rows.Opportunity: Daily bank reconciliation — the survey's top ask that never got airtime
rows.What Claude does: A written procedure Claude follows each morning: take the ANZ statement export and the NetSuite bank/GL extract for the same date range, match on date + amount + reference, and return only three lists — matched, unmatched in ANZ, unmatched in NetSuite — with a suggested coding for each unmatched line based on prior-month treatment of the same payee. Human confirms and posts.
rows.Notes: Why not raised: Person F read 'daily bank reconciliation' off the survey in the opening minutes and then the room immediately followed Person A into StockSys and Employment Hero. Bank rec is a solo, daily, quiet task — nobody in the room owned it out loud, so nobody defended it, and it never came back. It is the only named process phase on the board with zero opportunities attached to it.

rows.Opportunity: End-of-month statement and balance sheet reconciliation pack
rows.What Claude does: Point Claude at the month's supporting files and have it produce the balance sheet reconciliation working papers — one tab per account, movement explained, prior-month comparative, open items carried forward with ageing — plus a first draft of the end-of-month statement narrative for review.
rows.Notes: Why not raised: Both were named in the survey readout ('balance sheet reconciliation', 'repetitive tasks, like the end-of-month statement') and neither was ever unpacked. The room spent its energy on the two processes that had a person sitting in the room able to narrate the clicks; the close pack has no single narrator so it stayed abstract.

rows.Opportunity: Closing the loop on flag emails — chase, escalate, evidence
rows.What Claude does: After the mismatch emails go out, a weekly task re-reads the open flag list, checks the inbox for replies, and produces a short ageing report: which stores replied and resolved, which replied without resolving, which have not replied in 7/14 days — with escalation drafts ready for the ones that have aged.
rows.Notes: Why not raised: The room designed the send and stopped there. Person F even flagged 'following up on emails' and 'email chores' from the survey and said Person F'd need to know more — and never got back to it, because the conversation moved to systems. The unresolved flags are the actual recurring cost; the first email is cheap, the chasing is not.

rows.Opportunity: Offboarding mirror: the half of Employment Hero nobody described
rows.What Claude does: A procedure covering the exit side: from the departure notification, produce the offboarding checklist — final pay inputs (accrued leave, notice, any overtime outstanding), HR record closure in Employment Hero, access and asset list, and the confirmation that the person is removed from the next payroll run for their cycle.
rows.Notes: Why not raised: It was said out loud once — 'onboarding for all the HR and offboarding' — and then the room only ever built out onboarding. Terminations surfaced again inside payroll ('any termination if there's any — we do all that manually') and still nobody connected the two. Exits are irregular and unloved, so they never feel like a 'process' worth naming in a workshop.

rows.Opportunity: Leave and termination proration check inside the payroll review
rows.What Claude does: Extend the pre-submission review beyond hourly rates: check that each approved leave request in the period actually landed in the pay run at the right hours and rate, that terminations have correct accrued-leave payout and final-period proration, and that nobody appears in both the fortnightly and monthly run.
rows.Notes: Why not raised: The room explicitly scoped the review to hourly rate variations and waved leave through — 'it's in the system and we just do an upload… as long as that system is working correctly'. That assumption is the blind spot: the one input nobody verifies is the one that was described as automatic. Variations from leave were treated as noise to exclude rather than a thing to test.

rows.Opportunity: Payroll runbook as a standing Project — the Person R-and-me dependency
rows.What Claude does: A standing Project holding the payroll calendar, the definitive list of who is monthly versus fortnightly, cut-off dates, the click-path through Employment Hero for each step, the leave upload sequence, and the ATO/ANZ post-run steps — so every run is executed against the same written context rather than recall.
rows.Notes: Why not raised: Person F said it in the room — 'if Person F guys don't remember these, there has to be some sort of reference' — and the room answered the question rather than turning it into a build. Payroll is currently held by two named people; that felt like a fact about staffing, not an opportunity. Nobody named key-person risk because everyone in the room already knows the answers.

rows.Opportunity: Access and connector readiness audit before the 48-hour build
rows.What Claude does: Before building, walk each system and record: login ownership, whether multi-factor or token challenges block an unattended run, what can be exported on a schedule versus only clicked, and which steps must stay human-in-the-loop. Output is a one-page map of what Claude can carry unattended, what it can carry with a human present, and what needs a connector request.
rows.Notes: Why not raised: Every system on the board is listed connector-unknown, and the room accepted 'anything Person F can click on a browser Person F can tell Claude to click' at face value. It went unchallenged because it is broadly true — but the two highest-value endpoints raised are a government portal and a bank upload, exactly where step-up authentication and payment authorisation will stop an unattended task. Better to find that now than mid-build.

rows.Opportunity: Repeat-offender trend on warranty activation, by store
rows.What Claude does: A monthly rollup across reconciliations: which stores generate mismatches repeatedly, which SKUs or brands recur, whether a flag was a genuine misactivation or an accidental sell-out, and a short trend view showing whether a store's error rate is improving after being contacted.
rows.Notes: Why not raised: The room solved the month in front of it — find this month's mismatches, email this month's stores — and never asked why the same mismatches keep appearing. Reconciliation was framed as a finance accuracy task, so the operational cause sitting behind it (stores not activating warranty codes) never got an owner or a measurement in the room.
